channels.name: TikTok
channels.howGamesGrowThere: Discovery is interest-graph: a video from a 0-follower account can reach millions, so one hit clip drives a spike rather than steady growth. Documented indie outcomes: a single viral video typically yields ~1,000-2,000 Steam wishlists; sustained accounts (Mortal Rite) built 640k+ followers and 60k+ wishlists with zero ad spend. GameDiscoverCo's analysis of 1,500+ studio TikToks found likes/favorites correlate strongly with views, comments moderately, shares not. By 2026 several practitioners report TikTok organic reach for game devs weaker than Reels/Shorts, so cross-posting is standard.
channels.linkMechanics: Clickable bio link requires 1,000+ followers on a personal account, or a Business account (sources conflict: some say business accounts still need 1,000 followers, a 2026 guide says verified business accounts get links at 0 followers). Links are added via the mobile app. No clickable links in captions or comments for normal accounts, so the path is video -> profile -> bio link (extra tap = friction). Below the threshold, the URL can only be typed as plain text in the bio. Viewers are overwhelmingly on phones, so a 'play now' link must open a mobile-friendly web build or capture an email/wishlist; a desktop-only Steam page loses most mobile visitors at the click.
formatsThatWork: Raw, unpolished dev footage over polished trailers (practitioner consensus across TikTok/Reels/Shorts)
One clear hook/pitch readable in the first frame (A Game About Digging A Hole: 'dig a hole to find a secret')
Satisfying/tactile loop clips (A Little to the Left tidying puzzles spread via TikTok creators)
Physics/emergent funny moments (Webfishing avatar-launching clips spread on TikTok and X)
Dev-on-camera series content (Mortal Rite averaged ~498k views per video across its account)
Story/relatable-character hooks for narrative games (I Just Want to be Single visual novel)
channels.cadence: No hard sourced cadence benchmark found in this pass. Evidence implies volume matters: Mortal Rite's 126M views came from many videos averaging ~498k each (126.1M / 498k = ~253 videos, derived). Practitioner guides recommend posting the same clip to TikTok, Reels and Shorts because a clip that flops on one can hit on another.

benchmarks.metric: I Just Want to be Single single-video result
benchmarks.value: 571k views -> ~2,900 wishlists (~197 views per wishlist, ~0.5%, derived); doubled total wishlists to ~6,000
1,500+ game-studio videos; top performers totaled ~700M views; likes/favorites strongly correlated with views, shares not
~74% mobile / ~26% desktop for website visits (app usage is additionally mobile-only, so true mobile share is higher)

pitfalls: Views are spiky and mostly non-converting: ~2,000 views per wishlist in Mortal Rite's sustained case
No in-video/caption links; under 1,000 followers there is no clickable link at all unless using a business account
Mobile viewers cannot play a desktop/Steam game on the spot; intent decays before they reach a PC
2026 reports of weaker organic game reach on TikTok vs Reels/Shorts; do not single-home
Viral clips can attract an audience (e.g. meme/horror) that doesn't match a cozy game

channels.name: YouTube Shorts
channels.howGamesGrowThere: Same short clips as TikTok, but feeding a YouTube channel that also hosts long-form devlogs, so Shorts viewers can be converted into subscribers who later watch devlogs (where links work). In the A Game About Digging A Hole launch the same post did 2.2M views on Shorts vs 5M TikTok and 14.5M Instagram. One 2026 practitioner source says Reels and Shorts delivered higher organic reach than TikTok for most game creators it tested.
channels.linkMechanics: Since 31 Aug 2023 links in Shorts descriptions and comments are not clickable. Replacement: a 'Related video' link on each Short that points to one of your own long-form videos (devlog/trailer), plus channel-header links near the Subscribe button. Path for a play link: Short -> related long-form video -> description/pinned comment link -> game. Two hops of friction.
formatsThatWork: Cut-downs of devlog highlights with Related-video link to the full devlog
Before/after and progress clips that tease a longer video
channels.cadence: No sourced cadence number found; cross-post every TikTok clip here.

channels.name: YouTube long-form
channels.howGamesGrowThere: Devlog series build a compounding, invested audience and give the only place on YouTube where a clickable link sits next to the content (description, pinned comment). Proven devlog-driven outcomes: Jonas Tyroller's devlog audience gave Thronefall early players (game later ~1M copies year one, 565k wishlists); ThinMatrix (~254k subs) funded full-time indie dev via devlogs for Equilinox and now farming game Homegrown; DevDuck (160k+ subs) built a following for cozy 2D RPG Dauphin over 3.5 years; Dani's devlog channel made Karlson one of Steam's most-wishlisted games before release. Also: larger creators covering a demo (Gamescom/IGN + streamers for We Harvest Shadows; GameGrumps/Jerma for A Little to the Left) is the biggest lever and comes from YouTube.
channels.linkMechanics: Clickable links in description and pinned comment; end screens/cards link to other videos (external links in cards require YPP). Viewers skew more to TV/desktop than TikTok, so a desktop Steam/itch link converts better here than from short-form (no sourced split found).
formatsThatWork: Episodic devlog with a narrative arc and a clear stake ('I made a game in X days', 'my game failed / how it sold')
Problem-solving 'coding adventure' style deep dives (Sebastian Lague, 1.4M subs)
Game-jam / challenge videos (Blackthornprod ~597k subs, 65M lifetime views)
Postmortem/sales-number reveal videos (popular in dev community; also attracts devs, not players)
channels.cadence: No sourced cadence benchmark. Expanded YPP requires 3 public uploads in 90 days, a practical floor of ~1 long-form upload per month.

viralHits.name: Suika Game (Watermelon Game)
viralHits.platform: Nintendo Switch (Japan eShop 2021, global Oct 2023); many free web/mobile clones
viralHits.howItSpread: Boom from 15 Sep 2023 after Japanese live streamers, especially VTubers, played it; spread from Japanese influencers to overseas audiences.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Watchable runs: fruit physics chain reactions and near-miss collapses make good clips; score chasing between streamers.
viralHits.results: Developer Aladdin X said sales rose 'more than 50,000 times' versus before the boom; 1M Switch downloads in the month to 6 Oct 2023, then another 1M in 10 days (2M in Japan); reports say downloads later passed 10M.
viralHits.lesson: The developer credited cute, friendly art, very simple rules, and a 'try to do better next time' feeling. Physics-driven merging gives a different, clippable outcome every run, and streamers carried it.
viralHits.confidence: high for the 50,000x and 2M Japan figures; medium for 10M

viralHits.name: Wordle
viralHits.howItSpread: One puzzle a day for everyone. Players posted the spoiler-free emoji grid of green, yellow and grey squares on social media, which made people curious without giving the answer away.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Emoji result grid that shows how you did but not the word; shared daily streaks.
viralHits.monetization: None at first; sold to The New York Times for 'low seven figures'.
viralHits.results: 90 players on 1 Nov 2021, 300,000 two months later, then millions of daily players; the NYT said it brought 'tens of millions of new users'. Wordle had 5.3B plays in 2024 within NYT Games' 11.1B total.
viralHits.lesson: A shareable result plus one shared puzzle per day lets every share recruit new players. Keeping the game scarce (one a day) makes people come back daily.

viralHits.name: NYT Connections & Strands (daily puzzle portfolio)
viralHits.howItSpread: Copied Wordle's daily emoji-grid sharing and rode NYT's audience. Connections (June 2023) became the second most played NYT game after Wordle.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Coloured-square result grid; arguments about the day's 'purple' category.
viralHits.results: In 2024 NYT counted 11.1B puzzles solved: Wordle 5.3B, Mini 2.1B, Strands 1.3B. No Connections figure was found.
viralHits.lesson: The daily, shareable-grid format can be repeated across many puzzle types. A small portfolio of daily puzzles keeps people around.

viralHits.name: Framed (framed.wtf)
viralHits.howItSpread: Part of the 2022 wave of '-dle' clones; it took the Wordle loop (one puzzle a day, limited guesses, share grid) into a fandom niche, film fans.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Emoji result string showing how many guesses it took.
viralHits.monetization: Free web game; no monetization data found.
viralHits.results: Reported to have more than 1 million players every day.
viralHits.lesson: A niche theme plus the daily-share loop can reach a million daily players with tiny scope. Cozy versions could use plants, cats, recipes or cozy-game screenshots.

viralHits.name: Infinite Craft (neal.fun)
viralHits.howItSpread: The creator's X announcement got more than 15M views in a week. Clips of absurd combinations went viral, and Twitch and YouTube creators played it. Players were crafting almost 1,000 items per second by 2 Feb 2024.
viralHits.shareMechanic: 'First Discovery' tags and absurd recipe chains, posted as screenshots and clips.
viralHits.monetization: No revenue data found; neal.fun traffic was about 9.47M visits in one January month (Semrush).
viralHits.results: 15M+ views on the launch post; reported as the third most searched game of 2024.
viralHits.lesson: Combining things with endless, surprising results plus a bragging-rights 'first discovery' produces user-made content without any multiplayer.
viralHits.confidence: high for the views and craft rate; medium for traffic and search rank

viralHits.name: The Password Game (neal.fun)
viralHits.howItSpread: The launch tweet got more than 11,000 retweets and the site had over 1M visits on day one. TikTok gameplay reactions spread it: one video got 8.1M views and 1.1M likes in a month.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Reaction-friendly absurd rules ('rule 14...'); viewers want to try it themselves.
viralHits.results: Played more than 10M times.
viralHits.lesson: Absurd escalation with no tutorial works as a TikTok format: the viewer sees the twist and clicks through to try it.

viralHits.name: Draw a Perfect Circle (neal.fun)
viralHits.howItSpread: Viral after its Jan 2023 release; players shared their percentage scores on Twitter.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Single percentage score that is easy to compare.
viralHits.results: No play-count figures found.
viralHits.lesson: A 5-second game with one number as the result is a ready-made challenge clip ('can you beat 94%?').

viralHits.name: Stimulation Clicker (neal.fun)
viralHits.howItSpread: Released 6 Jan 2025 and called the 'first viral link of the year'. It rode the creator's existing audience and satirised internet overstimulation.
viralHits.shareMechanic: The chaos on screen is the joke, so screen recordings are the share.
viralHits.results: No numbers found.
viralHits.lesson: Once a creator has an audience, each new small web toy launches into it. A portfolio site that keeps shipping tends to build on itself.

viralHits.name: Cookie Clicker
viralHits.howItSpread: Written in one evening and posted as a link on 4chan; it reached 50,000 players within hours. Years of free web play built the fanbase before the paid Steam release.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Huge-number bragging; 'it's still running in my tab'.
viralHits.monetization: Free web with ads; paid Steam version.
viralHits.results: Steam review score 96% across about 92K reviews. Sales estimates conflict: about 2.5M copies / $10.8M gross versus about 6.75M / $33.7M.
viralHits.lesson: A free web game that keeps going can later become a profitable paid version: the web builds the audience and the premium release earns the money.
viralHits.confidence: high for origin; low for sales (estimates conflict)

viralHits.name: Universal Paperclips
viralHits.howItSpread: Word of mouth about its escalating AI-paperclip-maximizer story; it became the most cited browser game of 2017 despite plain unstyled text.
viralHits.shareMechanic: 'You have to play it to the end' recommendations; the story twist.
viralHits.results: About 2 million players.
viralHits.lesson: A strong idea and escalating reveals can beat production values. Incremental loops hold attention.

viralHits.name: Little Alchemy / Little Alchemy 2
viralHits.platform: Chrome Web Store / browser, later iOS & Android; on CrazyGames
viralHits.howItSpread: A long-tail classroom and browser hit, and the template Infinite Craft later built on.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Recipe hunting; guides and hint sites.
viralHits.results: No download or revenue figures found.
viralHits.lesson: Combining things is a durable, cozy-compatible loop that people play for years.

viralHits.name: Townscaper
viralHits.platform: Steam/Switch/mobile; later a free browser version
viralHits.howItSpread: GIFs of the generative architecture were very shareable. A free browser version came after the paid release.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Screenshots and timelapses of pretty towns.
viralHits.monetization: Premium on PC, Switch and mobile.
viralHits.results: About 100K copies in just over two weeks of early access; 380K on Steam; more than 500K across PC, Mac and Switch before the Oct 2021 mobile launch.
viralHits.lesson: A toy with no fail state, where every click looks good, is very easy to film. Players' creations become the marketing.

viralHits.name: A Dark Room
viralHits.howItSpread: The web version built a following, then the iOS port hit No. 1 in the UK (20K downloads in one day) and held the top premium spot in the US for 18 days.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Word of mouth about the mystery and reveal.
viralHits.results: 2.26M downloads in under two years. A co-creator reported $697,270 after Apple's cut, of which $191,810 net went to him.
viralHits.lesson: A web prototype can prove demand before a paid port.

viralHits.name: Sandspiel
viralHits.howItSpread: Satisfying particle visuals plus a public gallery where people share and fork creations.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Built-in save, share and fork gallery.
viralHits.results: No metrics found.
viralHits.lesson: Satisfying physics plus shareable creations make a calming toy that is easy to clip. A gallery turns players into content makers.

viralHits.name: Bloxd.io
viralHits.howItSpread: No-download Minecraft-style play for school and Chromebook audiences, on CrazyGames and its own domain.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Multiplayer with friends; building.
viralHits.monetization: Ads (CrazyGames gets 99% of its revenue from ads).
viralHits.results: Reported more than 15M monthly players and 8M+ registered accounts; 4.36M site visits in March 2026; about 14.8K concurrent players with a 27K daily peak.
viralHits.lesson: Familiar mechanics delivered instantly in the browser win the Chromebook and school audience.

viralHits.name: Slither.io
viralHits.howItSpread: Instant multiplayer with no signup and simple mouse or touch input. YouTubers and app-store charts pushed it with zero marketing budget.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Leaderboard length; streamer clips.
viralHits.results: More than $100K a day in ad revenue at its 2016 peak; 68M+ mobile downloads; 20M+ US downloads by May 2016.
viralHits.lesson: Instant start, one-input controls and a 'one more go' loop scale on ads alone.

viralHits.name: Krunker.io
viralHits.howItSpread: No-install shooter with modding; a large web audience.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Mods, custom maps, clips.
viralHits.monetization: Ads + cosmetics; acquired by FRVR in May 2022 (amount undisclosed).
viralHits.results: More than 200M unique players at acquisition.
viralHits.lesson: Browser games can be bought up by bigger companies. Player-made content (maps, mods) extends a game's life.

viralHits.name: Vampire Survivors
viralHits.platform: Started as an HTML5 browser game on itch.io; then Steam, mobile, consoles
viralHits.howItSpread: Cheap price, a one-button feel and screen-filling chaos made it ideal for streamers and YouTube.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Screen-filling power-fantasy clips.
viralHits.monetization: Cheap premium + DLC; free mobile with ads.
viralHits.results: 1M copies, then 2.5M by April 2022; reported around 6M on Steam plus 3M mobile downloads.
viralHits.lesson: A solo developer's HTML5 prototype can become a hit. A satisfying auto-play loop is very watchable.

viralHits.name: fly.pieter.com
viralHits.genre: Casual MMO flight sim, 'vibe-coded' with Cursor + Claude
viralHits.howItSpread: The creator built it in public on X, with daily progress posts to his large following. The 'made 100% with AI' story itself was the hook (100M+ views on X).
viralHits.shareMechanic: Build-in-public story; multiplayer link sharing.
viralHits.monetization: Sponsor billboards and branded planes sold to startups (in-world ads), not ad networks.
viralHits.results: $1M ARR in 17 days (creator-reported). Later reported around $138K MRR, though that figure came from a 2026 roundup.
viralHits.lesson: For an AI-assisted solo developer, the process (daily build videos) is the content. Selling in-world sponsorships directly can beat ad networks when the audience is your own.
viralHits.confidence: medium (self-reported; the later MRR figure is low)

viralHits.name: Grow a Garden (Roblox)
viralHits.genre: Idle farming / collecting with real-time shared events
viralHits.howItSpread: A 16-year-old built it in days. It went from 500 to about 100K concurrent players in two weeks, then rare-seed and mutation hype plus weather events spread on TikTok and YouTube.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Rare mutations and pets to flex; scheduled global events everyone shows up for; trading.
viralHits.results: Peaked at 21.3M concurrent players on 21 Jun 2025 and 22.3M on 23 Aug 2025. Reported about $12M revenue in May 2025 alone.
viralHits.lesson: A cozy, slow, idle farm can become the biggest game in the world when combined with rarity, trading and timed shared events.
viralHits.confidence: high for concurrent players; medium for revenue

viralHits.name: Steal a Brainrot (Roblox)
viralHits.genre: Collect-and-steal tycoon built on TikTok 'Italian brainrot' memes
viralHits.howItSpread: Built directly on a live TikTok meme (Italian brainrot characters), so existing meme traffic flowed into the game.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Meme characters; steal and raid moments.
viralHits.results: 25.4M concurrent players (some reports say 25.8M in Oct 2025), a record for any single game.
viralHits.lesson: Riding a live meme can get huge reach, but the game is tied to how long the trend lasts.

viralHits.name: Dress to Impress (Roblox)
viralHits.howItSpread: TikTok, driven largely by adult creators. The 'Pose 28' emote became its own meme; the official TikTok has 2.5M+ followers averaging 5–10M views per post.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Themed outfit reveal and voting makes a natural before/after clip format.
viralHits.results: 9.7B visits; concurrent peak reported between 1.5M and 1.73M (Dec 2024); won three Roblox Innovation Awards; made by a 17-year-old.
viralHits.lesson: Dress-up plus a theme and a reveal is a natural short-form video format.

viralHits.name: SnapStyle Dress Up (Poki)
viralHits.howItSpread: Named one of Poki's top performing games of 2025 alongside Plonky.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Players take a photo of the finished look and decorate it, giving them something to share.
viralHits.results: One of Poki's two named top performers of 2025; no play counts found.
viralHits.lesson: Dress-up with a 'take a photo' ending is one of the strongest cozy genres on the biggest web portal.
viralHits.confidence: medium (ranking from Poki's year-in-review via search summary)

viralHits.name: Monkey Mart (Poki)
viralHits.howItSpread: Poki front-page staple, top of Poki's Cozy category; walking around triggers jobs automatically, so no tutorial is needed.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Low; portal discovery.
viralHits.monetization: Poki ad revenue share; mobile ports.
viralHits.results: Listed first in Poki's Cozy category (4.6 stars); no play counts found.
viralHits.lesson: Walk-to-work idle management (grow, stock, serve, hire helpers) is the main cozy portal format.

viralHits.name: Bongo Cat
viralHits.howItSpread: Built on an existing meme; free; runs in the background while you type. Tradeable hat drops on the Steam Marketplace kept people running it.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Cat-on-taskbar screenshots; selling rare hats.
viralHits.monetization: Steam Marketplace fees from cosmetic trading.
viralHits.results: All-time peak of about 194.5K concurrent players (May 2025). Despite that, net revenue was only about $2K–$4K a month (Mar–Jun 2025) and the developer said it was not profitable.
viralHits.lesson: Ambient 'leave it open' games can get huge concurrent counts, but a free game with no strong monetization earns very little.

viralHits.name: Rusty's Retirement
viralHits.genre: Idle farming that sits in a strip at the bottom or side of the screen
viralHits.howItSpread: The new format (it sits at the bottom of your screen while you work) was the hook; it started the 'bottom-of-screen idle' trend.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Desktop screenshots showing the farm under work apps.
viralHits.results: 100K copies in about 5 days; more than 330K on Steam (GameDiscover); later reports of more than 500K.
viralHits.lesson: A cozy game that doesn't compete for attention (always on, multitasking) is a strong new form, and a browser tab can do the same thing.

viralHits.name: Placid Plastic Duck Simulator
viralHits.howItSpread: Zero marketing. It was picked up by large Japanese and Korean Twitter accounts and by YouTuber RTGame (2.75M subscribers).
viralHits.shareMechanic: Absurdly calm premise; 'look at my ducks'.
viralHits.results: 98% positive across about 20K reviews. Sales estimates range from about 410K to 1.45M (they conflict); more than 70K in the first months.
viralHits.lesson: A tiny, silly, peaceful game made at a game jam can go viral on its premise alone. A low price lets people buy on impulse.
viralHits.confidence: high for zero-marketing and RTGame; low for sales

viralHits.name: Is This Seat Taken?
viralHits.howItSpread: A demo plus a very clear premise (seat picky passengers) that works well as short clips.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Relatable 'who sits where' scenarios.
viralHits.results: About 165.9K Steam copies and about $1.4M gross (estimate, July 2026).
viralHits.lesson: Relatable social-puzzle premises (seating, packing, sorting) fit cozy players and are easy to explain in a 10-second clip.

viralHits.name: Cats & Soup
viralHits.howItSpread: Cute cats, ASMR sound and screenshot-friendly art; kept up by events and collaborations.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Cute cat moments; collection.
viralHits.results: More than 80M cumulative downloads (earlier 50M milestone); a 23% in-app and ad revenue lift after monetization optimisation.
viralHits.lesson: Cute animals doing cozy jobs, idle progress and ASMR make a durable recipe for both ads and in-app purchases.

viralHits.name: Block Blast!
viralHits.platform: iOS/Android (web clones like 'Blocky Blast Puzzle' chart on Poki)
viralHits.howItSpread: TikTok 'satisfying clear' and high-score clips; later official TikTok collaborations.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Score screenshots; combo clears.
viralHits.results: 40M DAU and 160M MAU by Nov 2024; 70M DAU and 300M MAU by Jan 2026.
viralHits.lesson: Satisfying line clears with no fail stress work at huge scale. Its web clone sits on Poki's Cozy and Trending lists.

viralHits.name: Sprunki (Incredibox mod)
viralHits.howItSpread: Kids shared songs they made on TikTok and YouTube. A hidden 'horror mode' twist and character lore created reaction and theory content.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Every mix is unique, so players share songs and react to the horror reveal.
viralHits.monetization: Fan mod; clone sites run ads (no figures).
viralHits.results: One YouTube gameplay video got 2.5M+ views in a month; no aggregate numbers found.
viralHits.lesson: A creative toy where every output is shareable, plus a secret to discover, spreads fast with young audiences on short-form video.

viralHits.name: Gartic Phone
viralHits.howItSpread: Streamers play it with chat and friends; funny drawing chains become TikTok clips (3.2M and 10.2M-view examples).
viralHits.shareMechanic: End-of-round replay of the drawing chain, which works as a clip.
viralHits.results: 707.6K followers on Twitch; individual TikTok clips with 3–10M plays.
viralHits.lesson: A built-in replay of player-made chaos at the end of each round makes clips without extra work.

viralHits.name: GeoGuessr
viralHits.howItSpread: Streamers and creators (e.g. Rainbolt clips) plus esports events; its World Cup peaked at 254,918 concurrent viewers.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Superhuman-guess clips; challenge links.
viralHits.monetization: Subscription (85–90% of revenue); free-to-play ended Feb 2024.
viralHits.results: 2024 revenue SEK 310.9M (+33%); about €21M revenue at a 45–50% margin (earlier report); 85M registered and 15M MAU.
viralHits.lesson: A browser game can support subscriptions once creators make it a spectator sport. A good clip format is worth more than features.

viralHits.name: Tiny Glade
viralHits.howItSpread: Constant work-in-progress GIFs and TikToks before launch (teasing even its Coming Soon page). Cozy, Sims and city-builder streamers played it, and players built shareable things like Helm's Deep.
viralHits.shareMechanic: Satisfying procedural building clips; recreations of famous places.

patterns.detail: One compact artifact (emoji grid, % score, photo of an outfit) that shows how you did and makes others curious. This drove Wordle's growth from 90 players to millions.
One shared puzzle per day gives everyone the same topic to talk about, builds streaks and brings people back daily. The format works across many themes (NYT: 11.1B puzzles in 2024).

patterns.detail: Systems that produce surprising, unique outputs (recipes, mixes, builds), so players make the content for you. 'First Discovery'-style tags add bragging rights.
Visible near-misses, chain reactions or comedic chaos that streamers react to. Suika's 2023 boom came from VTubers; Placid Duck took off after RTGame covered it with zero marketing.
Objects that bump, roll, merge or clear lines with juicy feedback. Watchable without sound and readable in a 3-second hook.

patterns.pattern: 'One more go' short loop with a visible score
patterns.detail: Runs of 30 seconds to 5 minutes; when you fail you instantly know what to do better. Suika's developer explicitly credited this 'try to do better next time' feeling.

patterns.pattern: Instant start, no tutorial, one input
patterns.detail: Clicking the link means you are playing within seconds, with no signup or download, and the controls are obvious (tap, drag, walk). This matters for traffic from a TikTok link in bio, where every extra step loses players.

Cozy games that live beside work or study (bottom-of-screen, taskbar, background tab) and reward you for keeping them open. They reach large concurrent counts but need a monetization plan (Bongo Cat earned only about $2–4K a month).
Cute animals and food, rules you can explain in one sentence, and a price low enough to buy on impulse (free web; about $2 on Steam).
Rare drops, mutations and cosmetics give people reasons to post and trade. Combined with cozy farming this drove the biggest concurrent counts ever recorded.

patterns.pattern: Build in public and the creator's own audience
patterns.detail: The making of the game is itself content (daily development clips, 'made with AI'), and every new release launches into the existing audience.
examples: neal.fun (Password Game, Infinite Craft, Stimulation Clicker)

patterns.pattern: Absurd escalation / premise as the hook
patterns.detail: A premise funny enough to explain in the video's caption, where the escalation is the punchline.

patterns.pattern: Web first, then a paid port
patterns.detail: A free browser version proves the hook and builds an audience; a paid Steam or mobile version earns the money.

sentiment.finding: GDC 2026 State of the Industry: 52% of industry professionals say gen AI is having a negative impact (30% in 2025, 18% in 2024); only 7% positive. 36% use gen AI tools at work.
By discipline, visual/technical artists (64%), designers/narrative (63%) and programmers (59%) are most negative (GDC 2026).

Quantic Foundry survey (N=1,799, Oct-Dec 2025): 85% of gamers negative toward gen AI in games, 63% picked the most negative option; most negative about AI art, music, sound, narrative, dialogue (i.e. visible/creative uses).
Circana PlayerPulse 2025: just over 25% of US players say gen AI use makes them less likely to buy (up from ~22% in Mar 2024) - stated purchase impact is far smaller than stated dislike.

Controlled study of ~10k Steam games released Jan-Oct 2025: AI-disclosed games got ~52.6% fewer reviews than comparable non-AI games (avg 4 vs 7 first-month reviews), after controlling for genre, timing, dev experience, publisher.
Game Oracle: for established studios with existing followings, AI use was associated with 40-60% lower sales; ~53% fewer reviews for high-potential titles.

Sulka Haro census of 53,597 Steam releases (mid-2023 to mid-2026): AI-disclosed games are ~1/3 of new releases but only ~10-27% of estimated sales (up from 3-6% in 2024) - underperform, but the gap is narrowing.

Cozy audience specifically: Librarian (cozy, Apr 2026) dropped to ~38% positive within 48h over AI-refined assets in just 4 images + proofreading; streamers cancelled; players asked for AI-free alternatives. It later recovered to Very Positive - visible AI art is the trigger, and cozy players are among the most sensitive.

Backlash pattern 2025-26: review bombing, cancelled sponsorships, boycotts, rescinded awards over AI art/voices (e.g. Party Animals AI contest entries May 2026; Kickstarter RPG forced refunds over 'slop art').

Code vs content: players and platforms treat AI-written code as invisible/acceptable (Steam exempts coding assistants from disclosure since Jan 2026; Playdate allows code assistants while banning AI art/music/writing); AI art/voice/writing is what gets flagged and punished. CODEX MORTIS' AI-first marketing drew hostility despite working gameplay.

marketEffects.finding: Steam released ~20,000+ games in 2025 (GameDiscoverCo: 20,558; SteamDB 20,008); ~half got under 10 reviews (6,608 with 1-9, 2,174 with zero).
AI-flagged Steam launches grew from ~13/month to ~530/month and account for 60-90% of all growth in Steam's monthly release count; projected to exceed half of releases by 2027-28.
AI-disclosed games capture a disproportionately small share of revenue (10-27% of sales vs ~33% of releases) - volume up, average outcomes down; 'AI slop' stigma attaches to the label.
Vibe Jam scale: 2025 had ~1,170 entries; 2026 had 945 entries and 240k+ players total - many builders, few breakouts; attention concentrated on winners and well-followed creators.
fly.pieter.com's success is widely attributed to distribution (Levels' ~600k X followers, Musk share) rather than technology; 404 Media headline: 'yours probably won't' make the same.
Analyst framing: AI lowers creation barriers so discoverability gets harder; originality, quality and audience connection become the differentiators.

moats.why: The single clearest determinant in the evidence: fly.pieter.com rode a 600k-follower account; most technically similar vibe-coded games got little traction. With 20k+ Steam releases/year, reach is scarcer than code.

The visible layer is what players judge and punish; AI art reads as 'mushy' (CODEX MORTIS) and triggers cozy backlash (Librarian). A distinctive, human-directed style differentiates from the AI-flagged third of Steam.

Iron Nest shipped with zero AI and topped Next Fest wishlists; itch.io gives a 'No AI' tag; AI-disclosed games get ~50% fewer reviews. Using AI only for code keeps you off Steam's disclosure entirely.

moats.moat: Speed of iteration + live building in public
moats.why: AI makes iteration cheap; Levels added features daily in public, turning development itself into marketing content. Speed alone is not a moat (everyone has it) but combined with an audience it compounds.
Originality and audience connection are cited as the remaining differentiators when creation is commoditized; a recognisable mascot/world can carry across many small games and short-form videos.

Poki explicitly rejects AI/template-heavy games lacking distinct personality and polish; 'almost right but not quite' is the top AI-coding frustration, so the last 20% of feel is where human effort shows.

workflow.practice: Use AI for code, keep it out of what players see/hear
workflow.detail: AI coding is exempt from Steam disclosure; human-made or licensed art, music, and writing avoid the label, the ~50% review penalty, and cozy-audience backlash.

workflow.practice: Scope to a single-file / template browser game first
workflow.detail: JS/Three.js browser games are where AI output is most reliable and deploy is trivial; start from a running genre skeleton rather than a blank page.

workflow.practice: Ship a playable v1 in hours/days, then iterate publicly
workflow.detail: fly.pieter.com v1 took ~3h and was improved daily with posts; jam-scale (1 month) builds win real prizes.

workflow.practice: Split work across agents by domain and write tests
workflow.detail: Void Balls: 8 parallel Claude Code agents, each owning a domain, with 88 test files, shipped in 10 days. Have Claude check integration between files before playtests.
Greybox prototypes with simple analytics (session length, retry loops) before investing in art; only scale the ones that show engagement.

workflow.practice: Test hooks with short-form video before/while building
workflow.detail: TikTok evaluates each clip independently so zero-follower accounts can go viral; devlog, before/after and funny-bug clips work; use view/save rates as a cheap demand signal per prototype.

workflow.practice: Don't market the game as 'made by AI'
workflow.detail: CODEX MORTIS's '100% AI' framing drew near-unanimous hostility; market the fantasy and the feel, disclose honestly where required.

workflow.practice: Review code that touches money/data; keep backups
workflow.detail: AI code often has security flaws; review anything handling payments/accounts; version control and separate experiments.

workflow.practice: Lock genre and Steam page early; collect wishlists
workflow.detail: Zukowski: finalize genre before the Steam page, launch the page early; demos well before launch help conversion.

aiRules: Use AI freely for code. Players can't see it, and Steam stopped requiring disclosure for coding assistants in January 2026.
Keep what players see and hear human-made or closely human-directed: art, music, voice, writing. Cozy players punish visible AI hardest (Librarian fell to ~38% positive over four AI-refined images).
Never market a game as 'made with AI'. Talk about the game. Disclose honestly wherever a platform requires it.
Speed is how you find a hit, not what protects it. What protects you is an audience you own, a recognizable art style, and recurring characters across games.

recommendations.platforms: Build every game as a small (<20MB) HTML5 web build so one TikTok/YouTube link lands players in-game instantly with no login or install. Use your own domain (PWA) as the link target and hub - with H5 Games Ads rewarded ads, an email/Discord capture and a prominent 'Wishlist the full version on Steam' button - and pick ONE portal strategy: either Poki (web-exclusive, but 100% of ad revenue on traffic you send and 90M+ monthly players) or non-exclusive CrazyGames + itch.io (PWYW/premium unlock). Treat the free web game as the demo and sell an expanded cozy version on Steam ($5-15), since cozy fans pay for premium and browser-to-Steam funnels (shapez, Cookie Clicker, Vampire Survivors) are proven. Note YouTube Shorts descriptions have no clickable links (use long-form descriptions, pinned comments, channel links and the Related Video link) and TikTok needs a free Business account for a bio link without 1,000 followers. Apply to YouTube Playables, TikTok Minis and Discord Activities as upside once a game shows traction; skip Roblox, Telegram and native app stores until a hit justifies a port.
recommendations.marketing: Run one capture pipeline with three outlets: film raw 9:16 clips of the game's most satisfying/cozy loop and progress moments, and post each clip to TikTok, YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels (Digging A Hole got 14.5M Reels vs 5M TikTok views from the same post, so don't skip Reels even if it wasn't planned). Every Short links via 'Related video' to a monthly long-form YouTube devlog whose description and pinned comment carry the play link; that devlog channel is the compounding asset that gives launches their first wave (Thronefall), while ad revenue at ~$1-4 gaming RPM is a bonus, not a business. Because short-form viewers are on phones and need ~200-2,000 views per wishlist-level action, the link must open an instantly playable mobile-friendly web build (or a free demo) plus an email/wishlist capture; switch TikTok to a business account or reach 1,000 followers early so the bio link exists. Favor small-scope cozy formats proven to spread (satisfying building/tidying, idle/desktop-companion, social hangout with clippable moments) and design in shareable moments so players create clips too. Track views->clicks->plays per platform with UTM links from day one, and cap content work (e.g. batch-film weekly) to avoid the solo-dev burnout of making videos instead of the game.
recommendations.viral: Build short-session cozy games around one satisfying physical verb: merge, place, stack, pour, decorate or sort. Each run should end in a shareable result, such as a score card, a photo of what the player made or decorated, or an emoji grid. A daily seeded challenge gives a reason to come back and a ready-made TikTok/YouTube Shorts format ('today's cozy puzzle, can you beat my score?'). Make the link playable in under 5 seconds on a phone with no signup, and add an element of discovery or rarity (a rare variant, a secret combination, a 'first discovery' tag) so viewers' own results become content. Post the AI-assisted build process itself as a content series. Dress-up/decorating, idle shop management and Suika-style merge puzzles are the cozy genres with the strongest portal evidence (Poki 2025 top performers and Cozy chart). If Poki's reported 100% revenue share for traffic you bring yourself holds, publishing there while driving your own social traffic may beat self-hosting ads; confirm the terms with Poki.
recommendations.ai: Use Claude Code aggressively for code (invisible to players and exempt from Steam's AI disclosure since Jan 2026) but keep art, music and writing human-made or carefully licensed, because cozy players are among the most hostile to visible AI and AI-disclosed Steam games get roughly half the reviews of comparable games. Treat speed as a prototyping engine, not a moat: build many tiny browser/web prototypes, post short clips of each on TikTok/YouTube Shorts, and only invest further in the few whose clips and playtests show real pull. The defensible assets are an owned audience (the fly.pieter.com lesson), a consistent hand-directed art style, and recurring cozy characters/world that tie every game and video together. Never market games as 'AI-made'; disclose truthfully where platforms require it, and monetize via web portals (Poki-quality polish) and cheap premium Steam releases once a concept has proven demand. Expect most releases to earn little - the 2025 Steam median was under 10 reviews - so budget time for marketing at least equal to build time.

ladder.goal: Prove people play and come back.
where: Your own site on free static hosting (Cloudflare Pages, Netlify or GitHub Pages): the link in every video
An itch.io page as a mirror: free, instant, with comments and built-in stats
money: Tip jar: itch.io pay-what-you-want or Ko-fi
Email or Discord sign-up on the game's end screen
setup: One HTML5 build that starts in under 5 seconds on a phone
Free privacy-friendly analytics (Cloudflare Web Analytics, Umami or PostHog's free tier) with a few events: start, finish, return
A tracking link per video (UTM tags)
moveUp: Clips beat your channel average and comments ask where to play
Players arrive from your links (hundreds, then thousands)
Day-2 return of 20%+ for daily games, or 5+ minute sessions for idle games
Players share results without being asked
ladder.kill: Below those signals after 10+ clips and a fair number of players: archive it and ship the next prototype.

where: Optional: CrazyGames (non-exclusive) for extra traffic and ad revenue
money: A $2–5 one-time unlock: full version, archive, extra series, cosmetics or no ads
Payment through a merchant of record that handles sales tax and VAT (Lemon Squeezy or Paddle, about 5% + $0.50 per sale) or itch.io's checkout (10% default cut)
A paid desktop download on itch.io ($3–7): the same HTML5 game wrapped with Tauri or Electron
Rewarded ads (portal SDK or Google H5 Games Ads) as a small floor
setup: Unlock codes or accounts kept simple (a code by email works)
A clear 'what you get' screen; never block the free daily loop
moveUp: A steady share of active players pay (rule of thumb: 1–3%; measure yours)
Revenue per 1,000 players stable or rising
Email list and Discord growing every week
ladder.kill: Plenty of players but almost nobody pays after two pricing tries: keep it free as a marketing game and move on.

where: Pick a portal strategy for this game: CrazyGames (non-exclusive, ~60% of ads, 70% of purchases) or Poki (exclusive on the open web; 100% of ads on traffic you bring, 50% on Poki's). Check whether Poki accepts games already live elsewhere before you publish anywhere
Apply to YouTube Playables, TikTok Minis and, for social games, Discord Activities (all invite or partner-gated)
money: Your unlock or paid download continues
setup: Portal SDK integration; their file size and loading rules
A monthly long-form devlog to keep your own audience growing
moveUp: Portal plays and ranking climbing steadily
A few thousand fans on email, Discord or followers who have played
People asking for 'more' or a bigger version
ladder.kill: Portal traffic stays flat through several updates: keep the game live, put your effort into the next one.

ladder.goal: Turn a proven game into a real product.
where: Phone-style games (daily, merge, collect, idle): iOS and Android apps; Apple and Google take 15% under $1M a year
Deeper PC games (co-op, builders, story): Steam. $100 fee, a 30-day wait after paying, and a 'coming soon' page for at least 2 weeks; build wishlists from your audience for months before launch
Later: consoles through a porting partner
setup: App store accounts ($99/year Apple, $25 once Google)
Steam page with GIF-led screenshots and a demo
moveUp: This is the top of the ladder: keep the free web version as the marketing funnel
ladder.kill: If the paid version underperforms, the web game and audience still feed your next game.
